options: Indexes that were recently dropped from the database
Cases where the optimizer built a plan and determined an index it doesn't have would have helped
A complete, verified list of every index a table should have
The fragmentation level of every existing index
questions.explain: It logs optimizer-identified opportunities from actual query compilation, not a guaranteed-correct index design.

questions.q: Why should a DBA treat missing-index DMV suggestions with skepticism rather than scripting them all as CREATE INDEX statements?
options: Creating any index based on this DMV is technically impossible
Missing index suggestions are always wrong and should be ignored entirely
The DMV is only available on Azure SQL Database, never on-premises
The DMV never accounts for the write-maintenance cost of a new index and can produce overlapping, non-optimal column-order suggestions
questions.explain: It's a real, documented limitation — the suggestions are leads for a knowledgeable review, not a safe automated action.

questions.q: An index shows a high user_updates count on sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats, but zero user_seeks, user_scans, and user_lookups. What does that suggest?
options: user_updates being high always means the index is missing, not unused
The index is critical and heavily used by read queries
The index is pure overhead — every write maintains it, but nothing ever reads through it
The index is corrupted and needs an immediate DBCC CHECKDB
questions.explain: Read-side usage counters at zero with heavy write-side usage is the classic signature of a candidate to drop.

questions.q: What generally characterizes a duplicate (or near-duplicate) index?
options: It's an index that exists on two different tables with the same name
It's an index on the same table whose key columns overlap heavily with another index, often just in a different order or with different included columns
It's any index with avg_fragmentation_in_percent over 30%
It's an index automatically created by SQL Server Agent jobs
questions.explain: Duplicates are redundant maintenance overhead — the same effective index kept twice under different definitions.

questions.q: Why is avg_user_impact from sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats not a complete justification on its own for creating an index?
options: It estimates read-side query improvement only, without weighing the added maintenance cost on every write to that table
It measures disk space savings, not query performance
It only applies to indexes that already exist
avg_user_impact is always 0 unless the server has been restarted in the last hour
questions.explain: A high avg_user_impact on a heavily written table can still be a net loss once index-maintenance overhead is factored in.
